en: The Ritual Manual for the Image of the Great Sage’s Joyful Twin-Body Vināyaka Deva, in one fascicle;
compiled by Jingjue.
I have now, based on the oral transmission from the mouth of Kengwang (Halgwang),
composed this secret ritual manual.
As for the iconography of the Twin-Body Heavenly King:
The two deities, representing husband and wife, stand embracing one another.
They are fashioned to be seven inches or five inches in height;
both deities have the heads of birds and the bodies of humans.
However, the male devas tie their faces to the right shoulder of the female devas so as to show the backs of the female devas;
likewise, the female devas tie their faces to the right shoulder of the male devas so as to look upon the backs of the male devas.
The heels of their feet are all clearly visible.
Their hands and feet are soft and supple, like those of a robust, well-nourished, and beautiful woman.
The male devas have no flower garlands upon their heads.
The male deity has a saffron-colored *kāṣāya* draped over his shoulders,
while the female deity has a flower garland upon her head but does not wear a *kāṣāya*.
Their hands and feet are adorned with necklaces and bracelets;
they likewise tread upon the feet of the male devas.
These two deities are both of a pale flesh color and wear red lower garments.
Each holds the other’s waist with both hands,
the right hand covering the back of the left hand;
at the tips of the middle fingers of the two deities’ right hands.
Bring it to the back of the middle joint of the left middle finger.
This gesture of embracing the image symbolizes craving for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
As for this craving for the six sense bases:
First, he touches her face and back with his nose;
second, he joins his chest to hers;
third, he embraces her waist with his hands.
Fourth, she embraces love with her belly;
fifth, she treads upon love with her two feet;
sixth, she wears a crimson skirt.
Because this specifically expresses respect and affection,
there are practitioners who create offerings for the six images of love and respect;
such a person will certainly gain the respect and affection of kings, ministers, queens, court ladies, and all other people.
Arouse a courageous and faithful mind;
do not harbor even a single thought of doubt or hesitation.
There are many, indeed very many, instances where such verification has been realized. If you wish to practice the method of harmonization to eliminate obstacles and difficulties:
One should fashion an image of the six-armed deity.
As for its form, it has the head of a horse and the body of a human, fully endowed with six arms.
Regarding these six arms:
That is to say, the upper left hand holds a sword,
the next hand holds a fruit platter,
and the lower hand holds a wheel.
The upper right hand holds a staff;
the next hand holds a *paraśu* (battle-axe);
the lower hand holds a noose.
Furthermore, there is an image with four arms.
Its form has a lion’s head and a human body, fully endowed with four arms.
That is to say, the first right hand holds a battle-axe.
The second right hand holds a plate of *modaka* (joy-balls);
the first left hand holds an elephant tusk or a *vajra*, and the second left hand holds a jeweled staff.
Furthermore, this is according to the *Amoghapāśa-krodharāja-avalokiteśvara-sūtra*.
Regarding the visualization of the four-armed deity:
this is Vināyaka-vajra, whose form consists of a human body with a head [of an elephant], fully endowed with four arms.
The left first hand holds a vajra;
the next hand holds a battle-axe.
The right first hand holds a noose.
Next, one holds a trident.
This is the ritual manual for the form and image;
it is capable of secretly selecting and bestowing the vessel.
Regarding this Great Holy Heavenly King:
because the Great Lord Maheśvara possesses a body of sovereign transformation,
the Secret Dharma states:
He is called the Noble Deva because he possesses mastery over the six supernormal powers;
he is called Maheśvara because he possesses mastery over wisdom;
and he is called the Twin-bodied Vināyaka King because he has accomplished the power of attraction.
He is named the Six-Armed Deva because he brings the five grains to fruition.
Furthermore, as stated in the sutras,
Maheśvara is the Sovereign of Wisdom.
When the Dragon King of the Great Ocean sends down rain,
he is able to distinguish and count every single drop,
understanding them all clearly within a single thought-moment.
Based on this holy teaching, because he possesses mastery over wisdom, he is called Maheśvara.
Furthermore, to clarify the form and appearance of the six-armed Vināyaka of the four directions:
The deity of the eastern quarter, Cūḍapanthaka, is also known as the Great General Mūtideva.
His form is like that of a celestial being,
and atop his heavenly crown is placed the head of an elephant.
With his left hand he holds a parasol,
and with his right hand he holds a sword.
In the south is the Deity of Food and Drink, also named the Great General Ruciraketu.
His form is like that of a celestial being (*deva*).
Upon his heavenly crown is placed an elephant head.
His left hand holds a lasso.
Holding a flower garland in his right hand,
the deity of the western garments is also named the Great General Mūrdhagata;
his form is like that of a celestial being.
Upon his crown is a dragon's head;
his left hand holds a bow,
and his right hand grasps an arrow.
In the north is Gajamukha, also known as Kanakagaṇapati;
his form has the head of an elephant and the body of a human,
and in his left hand he holds a white crystal bead.
The right hand holds a precious staff (*ratnadaṇḍa*).
Alternatively, he may be endowed with six arms as previously explained; furthermore, there is a form with six faces and six arms as described in the sūtra.
This method is kept secret: Pūrṇabhadra’s right hand holds a precious staff.

The ritual manual for the iconography of the two-bodied Vināyaka deity, in which the beloved son holds a three-pronged mallet in his left hand. Written on the second day of the fifth month in summer of the second year of the Jōwa era (the *ninsyu* year).
This original manuscript was sought from the possession of the Great Archbishop Jishun of Chikaku-in;
it was then collated, punctuated with national characters (kana), and ordered to be carved onto woodblocks by the monk Kaidō of Rinka at Hōzan. Recorded by [the scribe].
Verified once. Cishun.
